Lesson ☆

The go-around, done right

A go-around is a normal maneuver, not an admission of failure. Most pilots fly it badly because they decide late and then do everything at once. Here is the sequence, why it is in that order, and the mistakes I see most often.

On this page

Decide early The sequence Why pilots get it wrong How we practice it

Decide early

The go-around is easy. The decision is hard. Some triggers that should make the decision for you:

  • You are not stabilized on final: airspeed, descent rate, configuration or alignment are still changing inside the last few hundred feet.
  • The runway is not clear: an airplane, a vehicle, a deer, a taxiing student who has not looked up.
  • You balloon or bounce and the airplane is not settling.
  • Tower tells you to. "Go around" from ATC is an instruction, not a suggestion.
  • Anything at all feels wrong and you cannot say why. That feeling is data.

Say it out loud — "going around" — and act. Announcing it commits you and stops the second-guessing that eats altitude.

The sequence

The order matters because each step sets up the next.

  1. Power. Full throttle, smoothly but without delay. In the Cessna 182 the propeller control is already full forward from the before-landing checklist; confirm it with your hand.
  2. Pitch. Stop the descent first, then set the climb attitude. Expect a strong nose-up pitch with full power and landing trim — you will need firm forward pressure on the yoke. Add right rudder; the airplane will want to yaw left.
  3. Flaps. Retract to the intermediate setting immediately, then the rest in stages as you accelerate. Retracting everything at once from full flaps costs you lift when you have the least altitude to spare. The intermediate setting and the airspeeds for each stage: TBDPOH numbers.
  4. Trim. Once the pitch is under control, trim off the forward pressure. Do not try to trim first — fly the airplane, then trim it.
  5. Sidestep and look. If something is on the runway, offset to the right so you can keep it in sight and stay clear of a departing aircraft's path. Watch for the traffic that made you go around.
  6. Tell the tower. "Skylane 123AB, going around." At a non-towered field, announce it on CTAF the same way. Then fly the pattern again like any other.

Why pilots get it wrong

  • Hesitating. Waiting to see whether it will work out. It rarely does, and the go-around from 20 feet is harder than the one from 200.
  • Flaps before power. Dumping flaps at low speed and low altitude produces a sink you may not have the height to absorb.
  • Letting the nose pitch up. Full power, full flaps and landing trim will pitch the airplane toward a stall if you let it. Push.
  • Chasing the trim. The trim wheel is not a flight control. Fly with the yoke, then trim.
  • Forgetting the rudder. A left yaw at low speed with the nose high is how a go-around turns into a stall-spin scenario. Right foot.
  • Silence. The tower is planning around what they think you are doing. Tell them.

How we practice it

We fly go-arounds from three points: on short final at approach speed, from the flare, and from a bounce. We do the first ones with the rejection called well in advance, then I call them without warning. The maneuver is checked on the practical test as Go-Around / Rejected Landing in the Private Pilot ACS; the Airplane Flying Handbook chapter on approaches and landings has the reference description.

Read the balked-landing procedure in your POH before we fly, and know the numbers cold.
